🏗️ Avoidable construction errors eat around 21% of construction turnover, and in Sweden alone that's roughly €10 billion every year. More than 70% of that rework starts in design, and every study says the same thing: the fix is more time in design. But building regulations have more than doubled in the last decade, and compliance now eats 30 to 40% of design effort. So the architects who should be shaping the spaces we live in spend their time checking codes instead.

AI–BOB, our 2024 portfolio company, just proved there is another way. On VDMA in Eindhoven, a 90,000 square metre redevelopment led by OMA, one of the most influential architecture firms in the world, AI–BOB moved more than 1,000 hours of compliance work back into design over 8 months. Regulatory admin that used to take multiple days after every design iteration now takes less than a day. 570 apartments, 38 floors, 65,000 parameters, all checked every time the design changed. No delivery date moved. What moved was time.

AI–BOB doesn't design anything. It removes the reason architects can't. Compliance stops being a gate at the end of the process and becomes feedback while you draw. And this is just one domain, one country, one project. When the rest of the regulations follow, thousands of hours across every architecture practice go back to what they should have been doing all along: designing spaces humans actually want to live in. 

🫶 Huge congratulations to Elin Mårtensson, Petter Wallberg, and the rest of the AI–BOB team, and to Bozar Ben Zeev and the OMA team on this milestone!

Thanks Construction Summit for bringing the industry together around this year’s theme: Change & Innovation.

I had the honour of opening the main stage together with Fredrik Heghammar on Lessons in business development, innovation and AI.

We discussed the massive improvement potential in construction, where much comes down to how we manage information and data to truly scale knowledge. And that leading innovation today is less about writing perfect strategy documents and more about building organisations that test, learn, iterate, and scale. Which also requires rethinking business models and incentive structures so they don’t hold innovation back.

But maybe most important: start small, and scale what works.

I also had the opportunity to lead a smaller networking session on innovation with a selected group of participants, where the conversation focused on what’s ahead in our sector.

Most of the AI progress we’re talking about has happened in the past five years. That’s about the length of a construction project. So what happens in the next project cycle? And how do we build organisations that can learn and evolve at the same pace, so we can capture the opportunities? A great discussion and we could easily have continued for another hour!

And finally, it was interesting to see how aligned the industry was when asked: “Will AI be an obvious part of business development within 3 years?”

The response: 100% yes.

If we expect to be there in three years, let’s start testing and implementing today!

content:
A visit to Brescia made me think about making and the possibilities of what I call 'beta-architecture'.

With around 13,000 manufacturing companies, Brescia remains one of Europe’s largest industrial clusters. What struck me is that making things is still part of the city’s identity and future.

Cities change. Industries change. Buildings change. The question is not how to stop change, but how to make sure valuable materials, knowledge and production capacity remain in circulation.

As someone working on circular architecture, I believe the challenge is not to stop producing, but to produce differently: moving from linear consumption towards systems where materials can continuously be reused, remanufactured and transformed.

The same applies to cities themselves. Many urban areas, like some we saw in Brescia, need new programs and activities long before permanent development becomes feasible. This is where I believe in beta-architecture (something we've been building since our time at DUS architects): temporary architecture that allows cities to test ideas, activate places and build momentum for change. Not as a placeholder, but as a catalyst that evolves with the city and helps new futures take root.

Many thanks to Stratosferica and the City of Brescia for the invitation to the Urban Creative City-break, and to the inspiring group of architects, designers, researchers and city-makers from across Europe for the conversations and perspectives.

It's not that it was hard, but somewhere around docket 50 you misclick, and now you're checking all of them again.

I've started to think that typing is one of the strangest things we do as humans

Typing was the most effective transcription method (hence the typewriter), and when computers came around it was the only way to interface with them. But humans have always had a natural way of communicating: voice.

Every important decision I made on site happened because of a conversation, not what software told me. The software only came in to help afterwards. 

We don’t type because it’s the most natural way to explain what happened, we type because, until recently, it was the only way a computer could communicate with us.

Had computers understood us from the beginning, I don’t think we ever would have designed construction software around sitting at a desk and filling out fields.

For what feels like the first time, that can finally change. Instead of forcing people to work the way software expects, AI allows us to build software from a first principles approach, and we believe that is going to hinge on conversational voice AI. 

That’s the bet we’ve taken with Alloovium by building the site operations platform powered by voice.

But tbh it doesn’t really feel like we’re asking construction to adopt a new behaviour, we're just utilising the behaviour that was already there.

I’ve already seen some pretty wild voice-based use cases (one of our customers already had a sewing-machine pedal hooked up to Wispr Flow), and I'm very curious to hear what else people are trying with voice AI!

The most legally important document on a construction site gets written from memory, at 7pm, in the truck.

The site diary. The daily log. Whatever your site calls it.

When a delay claim blows up, courts don't want your expert's analysis. They want contemporaneous records. What happened, written down when it happened.

Neat handwriting. Zero evidence.

And every supervisor knows how it really goes. "Works ongoing as per schedule," five days in a row, backfilled on Friday with the same pen.

The person who watched the whole day unfold is the person with the least time and energy to write it down.

Internal teams at construction companies are building tooling that’s more interesting than almost anything coming from construction-tech vendors.

I’ve just returned from three months in the US, where I spoke with some of the contractors pushing hardest on AI. All are rethinking how software should support people on site, and making visible progress.

The contractors moving fastest had one thing in common: AI implementation was someone’s job. Some had software development resources that rivalled plenty of tech companies I’ve worked for (not Alloovium though)

The titles varied: But the job consistently came down to four things:

1. Connect the systems.

2. Identify workflow opportunities.

3. Drive adoption.

4. Keep it safe.

Simple to say. Technically, it isn’t.

Connecting systems means identity, permissions, APIs, project context and reliable data movement between tools that were never designed to work together.

Identifying workflow opportunities means understanding the operation deeply enough to decide what is technically viable, what should remain deterministic or human-controlled, and how success and failure will be evaluated.

Driving adoption means deploying into the places people already work, creating useful feedback loops and maintaining the system after the pilot ends.

Keeping it safe means provenance, access controls, monitoring, audibility and a clear boundary for human approval.

This isn’t a “pick an AI tool” role. It combines internal product, platform engineering and operational change leadership.

We haven’t seen the function formalised at the same scale in Australia, but the people doing parts of the job already exist. What they often lack is the mandate, team and technical operating model required to turn an impressive prototype into a dependable workflow.

I don’t think that gap will last long. This may become one of the most important technical leadership roles inside construction companies over the next few years.

“AI Lead” may age quickly, but implementation ownership won’t.

“There’s already too many construction tech platforms out there.”

No. There are already too many preconstruction platforms out there solving the same problems: faster takeoffs and better estimates.

And it makes sense. That’s where budgets are set and money gets committed so its the obvious target.

But what about the hidden problems? The things that go wrong on site that cause 80% of jobs to go over budget and over schedule?

It’s a $1.4 trillion a year problem that incumbents have attempted to solve for 20 years, but for 20 years the number has only increased and continued to get worse. Why?

A project can assemble 15–20 different companies and hundreds of people. All with different contracts, systems, priorities. All expected to operate as one team across ten platforms.

The plasterer’s waiting to close the wall. The plumbing test failed. The electrician’s on another job and isn’t answering. Meanwhile, the plans were revised meaning yesterday’s work needs checking again.

The site manager is jumping between calls, emails and systems, figuring out who’s finished and whether the next crew can start.

And that’s just one checkpoint. Imagine 70 on one plan. Hundreds of plans across a large project. Then a company running over 100 projects a year. 

Each needs its own checks, evidence and sign-offs. One revised drawing affects an entire floor. Someone has to work out what can proceed and who needs to act.

And when the project ends? That team breaks apart. Everyone moves onto new jobs with different people and too much of what they learned never reaches the next team.

Tech is finally at a point to solve this problem and it's the problem we’ve been mapping and building at Alloovium (YC S26) from the very start.

Connecting existing systems, getting richer information from site and carrying more coordination in the background, bringing people in when decisions are needed.

I'm talking full avatar. You jump on an onboarding call. Chat with it about its job. Give it a Teams chat, Revit license, etc. It'll be able to do any CAD or menial tasks and return it back to the firms.

2) AI workers will outperform everyone on CAD work.
The AI gets access to all past projects. It learns firm standards. It asks the right questions. Within hours it learns the rules. It catches mistakes on current projects (and even already delivered projects 😅). Any CAD button click will be faster and easier to do by chatting with the AI.

3) Every piece of traditional software in AEC will be replaced by an agent.
Every tool people use from automating tagging, dimensioning, clash detection, detail management, and more is going to become a tool the AI can call on your behalf. AI can write API code and complex backends already. Agent collaboration is only getting better. In a year you can probably have 10,000 agents run for the equivalent of a human-year each to automate anything.

4) The important work will still belong to people.
AI is spiky. The model labs have been training AI to be really good at clicking buttons and reading documents. Client relationships, high-level design decisions with complex human tradeoffs, and more are out of scope of a lot of these environments. AI will get really good at CAD and data entry. Designing these buildings and working with people will still be what people do best.

Our ArchiLabs Desktop product is a first step towards this vision. We want to reduce manual button clicks to 0. Architects, engineers, and owners didn't jump into AEC to click buttons, we jumped in to build. That's what AI can unlock.

In early September the models got really good at 3D. We noticed the bridge wasn't just moving data around anymore. It could finish the work in Revit by itself. A native family from a manufacturer's PDF. Routing. Every view in the set.

So the sync bridge became its own product, ArchiLabs Desktop. Basically by accident.

If you tried AI in a CAD tool a year or two ago and wrote it off, I get it. Our own version from last year would have convinced me too.

There's still a lot to get right. Auditability, control, never making stuff up in a set someone has to stamp. That's most of what we work on now.

But the drawings were the bottleneck in my first company, and this is the first time I've felt like we can actually do something about it.

content:
Exploring the capabilities of Nano Banana Pro

I’ve been experimenting with NanoBananaPro model to explore how far AI can support early-stage architectural design. 

Previously, I tested whether realistic 3D perspectives could be generated purely from a floor plan with Nano Banana, aiming to reduce the time spent on early modeling and rendering. At that time, I saw promising results, but mainly for simple layouts with minimal detail.
With a more advanced model now available, I decided to redo the same workflow. this time with a more complex floor plan. The idea was to see how much the technology has evolved and whether it can handle richer conditions.

Workflow
 • Exported a 2D floor plan from Rhino
 • Used Nano Banana Pro to generate:
 – a rendered-style floor plan
 – a living room view with spatial details
 – a dining and kitchen view in one frame
 – bedroom perspectives based on the same plan

The results show that Nano Banana Pro handles complex designs and high levels of detail much better than the previous model. It produced more realistic, high-resolution images with stronger spatial qualities. However, to achieve the closest alignment with the floor plan, I iterated each generation a few times, and that part of the process became time-intensive and repetitive. 
This is where it becomes crucial to test and understand each model’s strengths and weaknesses. Only then we can identify where and how each model genuinely contributes to the architectural design process, and avoid situations where they become counter-productive. 

My conclusion is that Nano Banana Pro is a strong tool for early-stage storytelling. For complex plans with many layers of detail, it still requires multiple iterations to reach the closest alignment with the floor plan. but the progress is clear, and the potential is exciting.

If you’ve tried similar workflows, I’d love to hear your insights. Let’s share and learn together.

content:
Can the AI help with complex things like sprinkler layouts and voltage drop calculations?

This demo has two automations:

1. Fire sprinkler layout + hydraulic check
It reads each room’s size and hazard type, calculates sprinkler spacing, places heads, routes mains/branches/drops, then estimates flow, pressure, friction loss, elevation loss, and pressure margin. Each head is marked OK/warn/fail.

2. Fire alarm voltage drop
It places alarm devices, assigns them to NAC/SLC circuits, routes cable through the corridor, calculates current, route length, wire resistance, voltage drop, end-of-line voltage, and device margin. It then selects the smallest wire gauge that passes.

At the end we can see nice summary reports and even CSVs showing all the calculations. The AI created these automations, but then the automations themselves are deterministic and repeatable, so any firm can refer back to them with confidence.
